title: Object storage and blobs
scopeHtml: Scope: S3-style design, chunking, multipart upload, presigned URLs, tiers and cost.

notes.title: What object storage is
notes.html:
Object storage keeps whole files ("objects") in a flat namespace of buckets and keys, accessed over HTTP. There are no real folders and no in-place edits: you PUT a whole object, GET it back (optionally a byte range), DELETE it, LIST by prefix. Each object has data, a key (photos/2026/11/cat.jpg), and metadata.

Compare with the other two storage kinds:

Block (EBS) File (NFS, EFS) Object (S3, GCS, Azure Blob)
Access Raw disk to one VM Mounted folders, POSIX HTTP API with keys
Edit in place Yes Yes No, replace whole object
Scale TB per volume PB, but costly Effectively unlimited
Cost per GB-month highest middle lowest (S3 Standard about $0.023)

Worked example. 50M users upload an average 2 MB photo: 100 TB. In Postgres BLOBs that would wreck backups and cache. In S3 Standard: 100,000 GB x $0.023 = about $2,300/month. The database stores only photo_key (about 60 bytes), so 50M rows is 3 GB.

Industry examples. Amazon S3 (launched 2006, many trillions of objects), Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, MinIO/Ceph for self-hosting. Dropbox stored files in S3 and later built its own storage system (Magic Pocket) once scale made it cheaper. Netflix keeps masters and encodes in S3.

Everyday analogy. A coat check: hand over the whole coat, get a ticket (key), return the ticket for the whole coat. You can not sew one button on while it hangs in the cloakroom.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing large binary files in the relational database.
  • Treating S3 prefixes as real directories (renaming a "folder" is copy plus delete of every object).
  • Assuming you can append or edit a few bytes.

notes.title: How an S3-like system is built inside
notes.html:
Three layers: a front-end API tier, a metadata service mapping keys to storage locations, and a data tier of many storage nodes holding the bytes.

Flow of a PUT:

  1. Load balancer and API server authenticate (signature) and authorize (IAM/bucket policy).
  2. Data is split into chunks (for example 64 MB or smaller), each written to several storage nodes.
  3. Metadata (bucket, key, size, checksum, chunk locations, version) is written to a strongly consistent, sharded metadata store.
  4. Only after enough copies are durable does the API return 200.

Durability. S3 advertises 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability: expected loss of one object per 10 million objects every 10,000 years. It comes from redundancy across at least 3 availability zones, checksums on every read/write, constant background scrubbing and repair when a disk dies.

Replication vs erasure coding.

  • 3x replication: 200% overhead, simple, fast reads and repair.
  • Erasure coding (Reed-Solomon k+m): split data into k data pieces plus m parity pieces; any k of k+m recover the object. With 10+4: overhead 40%, tolerates 4 lost pieces. Used for large cold data; costs CPU and slower repairs.
Object 100 MB -> 10 data shards (10 MB) + 4 parity shards (10 MB)
Stored: 140 MB (1.4x). Survives any 4 shard losses.
3x replication would store 300 MB (3x).

Consistency. S3 was eventually consistent for overwrite and delete until December 2020; since then it provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT, DELETE and LIST. GCS has had strong consistency for years.

Worked example. 1 PB of data: replication needs 3 PB raw; 10+4 erasure coding needs 1.4 PB, saving 1.6 PB of disks, around thousands of drives. That is why hyperscalers use EC for warm and cold tiers.

Decision gravity. Choosing replication for hot small objects and EC for big cold ones is reversible (background transition). The metadata store design (sharded, consistent) is the hard part and a one-way door; most object store outages are metadata or index-related, not data-related.

Industry examples. S3's internals are partly public (re:Invent talks: ShardStore, a Rust key-value storage node; formal verification), Facebook's f4 and Haystack for photos (Haystack packed many photos into big files to avoid a metadata lookup per photo), Ceph RADOS, MinIO erasure sets.

Everyday analogy. A library that tears each book into sections, stores copies in different buildings, and keeps an index card that says where each piece is.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the metadata layer is the bottleneck, not the disks.
  • Quoting eleven nines as availability; it is durability, availability is about 99.99%.
  • Confusing replication with erasure coding overhead.

notes.title: Chunking and multipart upload
notes.html:
Big files are split into parts that upload in parallel and can be retried individually. A single PUT of a 5 GB file over a flaky mobile connection would restart from zero on any failure.

S3 multipart upload:

  1. CreateMultipartUpload returns an UploadId.
  2. UploadPart for parts 1..N (each 5 MiB to 5 GiB except the last; up to 10,000 parts; max object 5 TiB). Each part returns an ETag.
  3. CompleteMultipartUpload with the ordered list of part numbers and ETags; S3 stitches them.
  4. AbortMultipartUpload frees orphaned parts. Add a lifecycle rule to auto-abort incomplete uploads after 7 days, else you pay for invisible parts.
# AWS CLI does multipart automatically over the threshold
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_threshold 64MB
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_chunksize 16MB
aws configure set default.s3.max_concurrent_requests 20
aws s3 cp movie.mkv s3://my-bucket/raw/movie.mkv

Worked example. 4 GB file, 16 MB parts = 256 parts. At 5 parts in parallel and 20 MB/s each (100 MB/s total) it takes about 41 s instead of about 200 s at one stream. If part 137 fails at 99%, retry only that 16 MB.

Resumable uploads and chunk design for your own service.

  • Choose chunk size by network: 5 to 8 MB for mobile (small retry cost), 16 to 64 MB for datacenter.
  • Content hashing: SHA-256 per chunk lets the server say "I already have this chunk" (deduplication) and verify integrity. Dropbox-style sync uses 4 MB blocks with hashes so a small edit uploads one block, not the whole file.
  • Resumable protocols: tus.io, Google's resumable upload (session URI, ask server for received offset).
  • Track state: upload_id, parts received, expiry, owner in a database or Redis.
// Android: upload part with retry; each part independent
suspend fun uploadPart(url: String, bytes: ByteArray, attempt: Int = 0): String {
    val resp = http.put(url, bytes)          // presigned URL for this part
    if (resp.isSuccessful) return resp.header("ETag")!!
    if (attempt >= 4) error("part failed")
    delay(500L shl attempt)                  // exponential backoff
    return uploadPart(url, bytes, attempt + 1)
}

Industry examples. S3/GCS multipart, YouTube resumable uploads, Dropbox 4 MB block sync with content hashes, WhatsApp media upload with resume, Netflix chunk-based parallel ingest of masters.

Decision gravity. Chunk size is reversible per upload, but changing a content-defined chunking scheme later breaks deduplication of existing data. Multipart adds state to manage (orphan parts); the alternative of single PUT is fine under about 100 MB.

Everyday analogy. Moving house with ten helpers carrying different boxes at once, and re-carrying only the one box that was dropped.

Common interview traps.

  • Using single PUT for multi-GB files.
  • Forgetting to abort incomplete multipart uploads (hidden cost).
  • Not verifying checksums at the end.

notes.title: Presigned URLs and direct uploads
notes.html:
A presigned URL is a temporary link, signed with your secret key, that lets someone do one specific operation on one object without having credentials.

Why: without it, a 2 GB upload flows client to your app server to S3, tying up your bandwidth, threads and cost. With it, the client uploads directly to S3; your server only issues the URL.

Flow:

  1. Client asks API: "I want to upload cat.jpg, 3 MB, image/jpeg".
  2. API checks the user, allowed type and size, picks a key u/{userId}/{uuid}.jpg, creates a presigned PUT URL valid for 15 minutes, and stores a pending record.
  3. Client PUTs bytes straight to S3.
  4. S3 event (ObjectCreated) triggers a Lambda/queue; backend marks the record uploaded, creates thumbnails, scans for malware.
// AWS SDK v2: presigned PUT, 15 minutes
PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder()
    .bucket("media-prod").key("u/42/9f1c.jpg")
    .contentType("image/jpeg").build();
PresignedPutObjectRequest p = presigner.presignPutObject(r -> r
    .signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(15))
    .putObjectRequest(put));
String url = p.url().toString();

Security controls:

  • Short expiry (minutes for uploads; reads maybe hours).
  • Fix the key server-side; never let the client choose the path.
  • Presigned POST policies can enforce a content-length range and content type.
  • Remember the URL is a bearer token: anyone who has it can use it until expiry. Use HTTPS only.
  • Validate after upload (type sniffing, size, virus scan); the client can lie about content type.
  • For downloads of private files, serve through a CDN with signed URLs/cookies (CloudFront signed URLs).

Worked example. 10,000 uploads/hour at 3 MB = 30 GB/h through the app server would need roughly 67 Mbit/s sustained plus connection handling; presigned direct upload cuts app traffic to 10,000 tiny JSON calls.

Industry examples. Instagram and Slack-style apps use direct-to-S3 uploads; Android apps upload via presigned URLs from WorkManager with retry; CloudFront signed URLs protect Netflix-like paid content; GCS "signed URLs" are the same idea.

Decision gravity. Reversible and recommended default. Alternative is proxying through the app, only sensible for tiny files or when you must inspect bytes inline.

Everyday analogy. A valet ticket valid for one car, for one hour, which any person holding it can use.

Common interview traps.

  • Long-lived presigned URLs (days) that leak.
  • Trusting the client's content type or size.
  • Not handling the case where a client gets a URL but never uploads (pending records need a cleanup job).

notes.title: Storage classes, lifecycle, CDN and cost
notes.html:
Not all data is accessed equally, so object stores offer tiers with different price and retrieval cost.

S3 tiers (prices approximate, check current): Standard (about $0.023/GB-month), Standard-IA/infrequent (about $0.0125, retrieval fee, 30-day minimum), Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive (down to about $0.001/GB-month, retrieval takes minutes to 12+ hours), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-moves by access).

Lifecycle rule example.

{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "tier-and-expire",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": {"Prefix": "logs/"},
    "Transitions": [
      {"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"},
      {"Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}
    ],
    "Expiration": {"Days": 365},
    "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": {"DaysAfterInitiation": 7}
  }]
}

Serving files. Put a CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly) in front: edge cache hit ratio of 95% means 20x fewer origin requests and much cheaper egress. Set Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable and use content-hashed keys (app.3f9a.js) so you never need to invalidate.

Request limits and key design. S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix, and scales by prefix. Old advice to randomize key prefixes is no longer needed, but spread heavy traffic across prefixes anyway. LIST is slow and costly; keep an index in a database for queries like "all photos of user 42".

Other features: versioning (undo overwrite/delete), object lock (WORM compliance), cross-region replication (disaster recovery), server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or KMS), event notifications.

Worked example. 500 TB of logs. All Standard: 500,000 x 0.023 = $11,500/month. After 90 days 90% sits in Glacier at ~$0.004: 450,000 x 0.004 + 50,000 x 0.023 = 1,800 + 1,150 = $2,950/month, a 74% saving.

Industry examples. Netflix and Spotify tier old data; CDN-fronted images at Instagram; Cloudflare R2 markets zero egress fees as differentiator.

Decision gravity. Lifecycle rules are reversible but retrieval from Glacier is slow/expensive, so a wrongly archived "hot" dataset hurts. Egress cost (about $0.09/GB out to the internet on S3) is the hidden big bill; a CDN or private connectivity reduces it.

Everyday analogy. Keeping this week's clothes in the wardrobe, last season's in the loft, and old school books in a storage unit across town.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring egress and request costs.
  • Using LIST as a database.
  • Forgetting versioned buckets keep deleted data (and bills).
  • Archiving data that is read frequently.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Object storage = keys to whole immutable objects over HTTP; cheap, huge, durable; not a filesystem, no in-place edit.
  • Inside: API tier, strongly consistent sharded metadata, chunked data with replication or erasure coding across AZs.
  • Multipart upload: parallel, resumable parts (5 MiB to 5 GiB, up to 10,000), abort leftovers, checksum chunks.
  • Presigned URLs send bytes straight to storage; keep them short-lived, fix keys server-side, validate afterwards.
  • Control cost with lifecycle tiers, CDN caching and attention to egress; keep a DB index instead of LIST.

questions.subtopic: Object vs block vs file storage
questions.promptHtml: Why would you store user photos in S3 instead of the Postgres database or a mounted file system? What do you give up?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you pick storage by access pattern and cost, not habit, and know the limits (no in-place edit, no folders).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Photos are large, immutable, read whole, and there are millions of them. Object storage is the cheapest per GB, scales almost without limit and serves bytes over HTTP, so I keep the bytes there and only a small key in Postgres. I give up in-place edits, real folders, POSIX semantics and low-latency random writes: you replace the whole object.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three storage models:

Block (EBS)   raw disk attached to one VM, edit any byte, highest $/GB
File (NFS)    shared folders + POSIX, edit in place, middle $/GB
Object (S3)   bucket + key -> whole object over HTTP, lowest $/GB, replace only

Postgres BLOBs make the table huge, bloat backups, WAL and replication, and fill the buffer cache with bytes nobody joins on. 50M photos at 2 MB is 100 TB: about $2,300/month in S3 Standard, while the DB only stores a ~60 byte key (3 GB for 50M rows). The flat namespace means "folders" are just key prefixes: renaming a prefix is copy plus delete of every object under it.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting multi-MB blobs into the OLTP database.
  • Treating prefixes as directories and planning a cheap "rename folder".
  • Assuming you can append or patch a few bytes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you list all photos of user 42? -> Not with LIST; keep an index table (user_id, key) in the DB.
  2. When is a file system still right? -> Apps needing POSIX, locking or in-place edits (shared home dirs, legacy software).
  3. When would block storage win? -> Databases and anything needing low-latency random writes on one host.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "S3 is cheaper". The senior adds the access pattern (write once, read whole), the operational cost of blobs in the DB (backups, replication lag, cache pollution), and the metadata-in-DB pointer pattern with its failure modes (orphan objects, dangling keys).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that kept receipts as BYTEA saw nightly pg_dump grow from 20 minutes to 6 hours and replicas lag during uploads; moving blobs to object storage fixed both.

questions.promptHtml: How does an S3-like system achieve eleven nines of durability, and when would you choose erasure coding over 3x replication?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of durability mechanics and the cost/CPU/repair trade-off, and whether you confuse durability with availability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Durability comes from redundancy across failure domains (at least 3 AZs), checksums on every read and write, and constant scrubbing and repair after a disk dies. Replication is simple and fast to read and repair but costs 3x. Erasure coding such as 10+4 costs 1.4x and survives 4 lost pieces, at the price of CPU and slower, more network-heavy repair, so I use it for big, cold, mostly-read data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
100 MB object
3x replication : 3 copies x 100 MB       = 300 MB  (200% overhead)
EC 10+4        : 10 data + 4 parity x 10 MB = 140 MB  (40% overhead), any 10 of 14 rebuild it

Eleven nines means an expected loss of one object per 10 million objects per 10,000 years; it is a modelled number from failure rates, repair time and independence of failure domains. The key lever is repair time: the faster you re-create lost shards, the smaller the window for correlated failures. EC repair reads k pieces to rebuild one, so a failed disk causes much more network traffic than copying a replica. At 1 PB, replication needs 3 PB raw, EC 10+4 needs 1.4 PB, saving 1.6 PB of disks.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting eleven nines as availability (S3 Standard availability is about 99.99%).
  • Assuming EC is free: small objects get poor efficiency and reads may fan out to many nodes.
  • Putting all shards in one AZ and calling it durable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not EC for everything? -> Small hot objects: fan-out reads, CPU, repair storms. Replicate hot data, EC cold data, transition in the background.
  2. What does scrubbing do? -> Reads data in the background, verifies checksums, repairs bit rot before a second failure lands.
  3. How do you place shards? -> Spread across disks, racks and AZs so one failure domain loses at most m shards.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "it keeps 3 copies". The senior explains the overhead arithmetic, repair bandwidth, failure-domain placement and that most real outages are metadata/index problems, not lost bytes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A self-hosted MinIO cluster with EC 8+4 on one rack lost an entire rack's power and became unreadable until the rack returned: the code was fine, the placement was not.

questions.contextHtml:
A profile-photo service issues presigned PUT URLs. Security review flags this endpoint. Read it.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@PostMapping("/upload-url")
public Map<String, String> uploadUrl(@RequestParam String path,
                                     @RequestParam String contentType) {
    PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder()
        .bucket("media-prod").key(path)
        .contentType(contentType).build();
    String url = presigner.presignPutObject(r -> r
        .signatureDuration(Duration.ofDays(7))
        .putObjectRequest(put)).url().toString();
    return Map.of("url", url);
}
@PostMapping("/upload-url")
fun uploadUrl(@RequestParam path: String, @RequestParam contentType: String): Map<String, String> {
    val put = PutObjectRequest.builder()
        .bucket("media-prod").key(path)
        .contentType(contentType).build()
    val url = presigner.presignPutObject { it
        .signatureDuration(Duration.ofDays(7))
        .putObjectRequest(put) }.url().toString()
    return mapOf("url" to url)
}

The endpoint has no auth check beyond a logged-in session. Uploads land in the same bucket that serves the public CDN.
questions.promptHtml: List every problem and give the corrected design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Shorten the expiry." It misses that the client picks the key (overwrite anyone's file or write ../../app/config.js-like paths into served prefixes), that contentType and size are client-controlled, and that nothing validates after upload.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who may upload what (only own avatar)? Max size? Is the bucket origin of a public CDN (then an uploaded HTML file becomes stored XSS on our domain)? Any malware scanning today?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce expiry now, restrict the endpoint to the logged-in user, and stop serving the upload prefix from the public CDN until validated.
  3. Hypotheses (issues), ranked: client-chosen key (overwrite or write into trusted prefixes); 7 day bearer token that leaks via logs and referrers; client-chosen content type (HTML or SVG served from our origin); no size limit; no post-upload validation or cleanup of never-used URLs.
  4. How I'd verify: Try uploading index.html with text/html to a path under the CDN prefix; check CloudTrail data events for overwrites; test whether a 5 GB PUT is accepted.
  5. Root cause: Authorization was done at URL issuance only and the URL carried too much freedom.
  6. Fix: Server picks the key u/{userId}/{uuid}.jpg, expiry 5 to 15 minutes, a presigned POST policy with content-length-range and an allowed content type, upload into a quarantine bucket/prefix, an ObjectCreated event triggers sniff-by-magic-bytes, size check, malware scan and re-encode, then promote to the public prefix. Pending records get a cleanup job.
  7. Prevention: Bucket policy denying public read on the quarantine prefix, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, serve user content from a separate domain, a test that the issuing endpoint never accepts a key parameter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not proxy bytes through the app just for validation (it kills the bandwidth benefit); I accept post-upload validation latency of seconds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can you revoke a presigned URL? -> Not individually; it is valid until expiry or until the signing credentials are rotated or the IAM policy denies. Hence short expiry.
  • User uploads then swaps content after validation? -> Presigned PUT can be reused until expiry; validate by object version or ETag, or make the key single-use and deny overwrite via a conditional write if available (verify provider support).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a client-supplied path let an attacker overwrite a JavaScript bundle in a bucket fronted by the CDN. Fix was server-chosen keys and separate buckets for code and user content.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only "shorter expiry".
  • Hire: server-side key, validation, expiry, size limits.
  • Strong hire: quarantine bucket, separate domain, magic-byte validation, abuse and cleanup reasoning.

questions.contextHtml: A photo app gets 1M uploads/day averaging 2 MB, kept forever. Finance asks for a 12-month storage bill forecast and ways to cut it. Product says photos older than 30 days are viewed rarely (under 5% ever). Prices: Standard about $0.023/GB-month, Standard-IA about $0.0125/GB-month (30-day minimum, retrieval fee per GB: verify current). Ignore request and egress cost for now.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate month-12 storage cost with and without tiering and say what you would check before turning tiering on.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Glacier for everything old." It ignores retrieval latency for a user scrolling old photos and small-object and minimum-duration charges.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are thumbnails stored too (usually small, keep hot)? Delete rate? Is 5% of old photos of data or of requests? Is an access-latency of milliseconds required for old photos?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; first compute the baseline.
  3. Hypotheses (options): Standard only; Standard then IA at 30 days; Intelligent-Tiering (auto, with a small per-object monitoring fee: verify); Glacier tiers (too slow for user-facing reads).
  4. How I'd verify: Turn on S3 Storage Lens or access logs for 2 weeks and compute the age distribution of GETs.
  5. Math: Per day 1M x 2 MB = 2 TB. After 12 months about 730 TB = 730,000 GB. Standard only: 730,000 x 0.023 = about $16,800/month. Tiered: last 30 days 60 TB in Standard = 60,000 x 0.023 = $1,380; 670 TB in IA = 670,000 x 0.0125 = $8,375; total about $9,755/month, a 42% saving. Retrieval: if 5% of 670 TB is read per month, that is about 33,500 GB times the per-GB IA retrieval fee (verify, order of $0.01): about $335, small.
  6. Fix: Lifecycle rule transition at 30 days, plus abort-incomplete-multipart at 7 days. For uncertain patterns use Intelligent-Tiering.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of cost per tier, alert on retrieval-fee spikes, review quarterly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Glacier Flexible for user-facing photos (minutes to hours retrieval) and would not tier tiny thumbnails (minimum billable size and per-request transition cost).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if viewing old photos is 30% of traffic? -> IA retrieval fees and per-GB charges grow; compute the break-even: IA saves 0.0105/GB-month, so reads beyond roughly one full read per month per object erase the saving.
  • Transition cost for 1M objects/day? -> A per-request lifecycle transition fee applies (verify); with 2 MB objects it is negligible, with 5 KB objects it would not be.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team tiered 100 million 20 KB thumbnails to IA and the transition and minimum-size charges exceeded the saving; they tiered only originals.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers.
  • Hire: correct baseline and tiered estimate, mentions access patterns.
  • Strong hire: break-even logic, minimum size and duration, retrieval fees, request-level data to decide.

questions.contextHtml:
Month-end bill: S3 storage is $3,600 above forecast. The bucket inventory report shows 120 TB of objects, but billing shows 158 TB-months. Mobile uploads of 1 to 4 GB videos use multipart with 16 MB parts. Android crash rate on the upload screen was elevated after release 8.4.

$ aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket media-prod --max-items 5
Uploads: [ {Initiated: 2026-08-02, Key: raw/u/881/...mp4, UploadId: ...}, ... ]
count older than 30 days: 9,412

Nothing visible in the console object list explains the gap.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the gap, fix it, and prevent it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Maybe versioning is on." It checks the wrong place and never thinks of invisible, incomplete multipart parts that are billed but not listed as objects.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is versioning on (noncurrent versions)? Any lifecycle rules? When did the gap start (matches release 8.4)? How many uploads are in progress legitimately?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Abort uploads older than 7 days with a script, after confirming none is active.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: incomplete multipart uploads from crashed clients (38 TB gap, matches 9,412 uploads at roughly 4 GB); noncurrent versions; replication copies; delete markers.
  4. How I'd verify: list-multipart-uploads and list-parts to sum part sizes; Storage Lens "incomplete MPU bytes" metric; compare with list-object-versions counts to exclude versions.
  5. Root cause: Each CreateMultipartUpload succeeded and parts were uploaded, but the app crashed or was killed before Complete or Abort. Parts stay stored and billed until aborted. Nothing in the bucket had an abort lifecycle rule.
  6. Fix: Short term: bulk abort-multipart-upload for old IDs. Long term: lifecycle rule AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload after 7 days; client resumes via stored UploadId (WorkManager) instead of starting new uploads on each retry; server tracks upload sessions with expiry.
{ "Rules": [{ "ID": "abort-mpu", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": ""},
  "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": {"DaysAfterInitiation": 7} }] }
  1. Prevention: Alert on incomplete MPU bytes, a canary that kills the app mid-upload, review rule in the bucket-creation Terraform module.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A 7 day window means a user who resumes after 8 days restarts; I would not set 1 day because flaky-network users pause uploads overnight.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the S3 console not show it? -> Parts are not objects until Complete; they appear only in multipart listings.
  • Would a crash-looping client cause 1 UploadId per retry? -> Yes, if it calls Create each time; persist the UploadId and ask the server for received parts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a nightly ingest job aborted on timeout and left 200 TB of partial uploads for a year because the lifecycle rule lived in a different team's template.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames versioning without evidence.
  • Hire: finds incomplete MPU, adds lifecycle abort.
  • Strong hire: quantifies, fixes client resume logic, adds metrics and Terraform guard.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how multipart upload works, how you would make a mobile upload resumable, and how part size is chosen.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Resumable large uploads are a staple of media and file products; the answer shows state design, retry and integrity thinking.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start an upload session and get an UploadId, upload numbered parts in parallel, each returning an ETag, then complete with the ordered list. A failed part is retried alone. For resumability I persist the UploadId and finished parts and ask the server which parts it has before continuing. I pick 5 to 8 MB parts on mobile and larger in a datacenter, and verify checksums at the end.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
S3 rules: parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB (last part may be smaller), up to 10,000 parts, object up to 5 TiB. So for a 5 TB object part size must be at least about 0.5 GB.

Create -> UploadId
UploadPart(1..N)  parallel, each returns ETag
Complete(UploadId, [(1,etag1)...(N,etagN)])   or   Abort(UploadId)

Worked time: 4 GB at 16 MB is 256 parts; 5 parallel streams at 20 MB/s each give 100 MB/s, about 41 s versus about 200 s sequential. Part loss at 99% costs one 16 MB retry, not 4 GB. Smaller parts mean cheaper retries but more requests and more state; larger parts mean fewer calls but expensive retries. Content hashes per chunk let you skip chunks the server already has (deduplication) and detect corruption. Cleanup: lifecycle abort rule, or you pay for invisible parts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
String uploadPart(HttpClient http, URI presignedPartUrl, byte[] bytes) throws Exception {
    for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
        HttpResponse<Void> r = http.send(
            HttpRequest.newBuilder(presignedPartUrl).PUT(BodyPublishers.ofByteArray(bytes)).build(),
            BodyHandlers.discarding());
        if (r.statusCode() == 200) return r.headers().firstValue("ETag").orElseThrow();
        if (attempt >= 4) throw new IllegalStateException("part failed");
        Thread.sleep(500L << attempt); // exponential backoff
    }
}
suspend fun uploadPart(url: String, bytes: ByteArray, attempt: Int = 0): String {
    val resp = http.put(url, bytes)
    if (resp.isSuccessful) return resp.header("ETag")!!
    if (attempt >= 4) error("part failed")
    delay(500L shl attempt)
    return uploadPart(url, bytes, attempt + 1)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Single PUT for multi-GB files.
  • No abort rule for orphaned uploads.
  • Retrying without backoff and jitter, causing a retry storm on a degraded network.
  • Skipping final integrity verification.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you keep upload state? -> DB or Redis keyed by upload_id with parts, owner, expiry; the client also stores it locally.
  2. How do presigned URLs fit? -> One presigned URL per part, issued by the API after authorization.
  3. Dropbox-style sync of a 1 GB file with a small edit? -> Content-defined or fixed 4 MB blocks with hashes; upload only changed blocks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists the three API calls. The senior adds part limits and part-size math, parallelism versus mobile battery and bandwidth, idempotent retries, checksum verification, orphan cost and session expiry.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A video app's uploads failed at 98% on bad networks until it moved from single PUT to 8 MB resumable parts; completion rate rose sharply and support tickets dropped.

questions.contextHtml: Product manager: "Let users upload videos from their phones. Should be fast and reliable." No further detail. Expected 200k DAU, 5% upload one video per day.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Immediately draws app server receiving the file and writing to S3. It never asks about size, network, or what happens after upload.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max length and size (say 2 GB)? Must uploads resume after app kill? Is processing (transcoding, moderation) needed before publishing? Is content private or public? Regions and data residency? What does "fast" mean: time to publish or upload speed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I state assumptions explicitly: 10k uploads/day, average 300 MB, peak 5x.
  3. Hypotheses (design options): proxy through the app (rejected: 3 TB/day through servers); presigned multipart direct to object storage (chosen); a tus-style resumable server (only if we need non-S3 backends).
  4. How I'd verify: Capacity: 10k x 300 MB = 3 TB/day = about 35 MB/s average, 175 MB/s at peak, trivial for S3 but heavy for app servers. Prototype resume on airplane-mode toggling.
  5. Design: API creates an upload session (id, owner, expected size, mime), returns multipart UploadId and presigned part URLs on demand. Client uploads 8 MB parts, parallelism 3, persists state in WorkManager or a background URLSession. Complete call, ObjectCreated event, queue, then scan and transcode workers, status processing -> ready.
  6. Fix (hardening): Per-user quotas, abort rule at 7 days, pending-session cleanup, idempotent Complete, checksums.
  7. Prevention: Metrics: completion rate, resume rate, time to ready.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make users wait for transcoding on the upload request, and I would not build a custom chunk server before S3 multipart proves insufficient.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 10x scale? -> Still object storage; scale the workers and queue, and watch per-prefix request rates.
  • Upload from the web? -> Same presigned parts with a JS client; CORS on the bucket.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped proxy uploads and paid for 40 extra app servers during a campaign; presigned direct upload removed them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proxying through the app with no questions.
  • Hire: presigned multipart, async processing.
  • Strong hire: clarifies first, shows capacity math, resume state, cleanup, abuse controls.

questions.contextHtml: A data platform has 200 TB of Parquet event files in S3 Standard ($4,600/month). A cost project adds a lifecycle rule: transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days. Two weeks later the data science team reports that backfill jobs fail with InvalidObjectState and the bill shows a retrieval spike. Their weekly model-training job reads 20% of last 6 months data.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how do you fix it without more disruption?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the rule." It is right but incomplete: it ignores objects already transitioned, restore cost and timing, and the minimum storage duration charges.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who reads which prefixes and how often? Required read latency? How many objects were transitioned and what object sizes? Any compliance retention?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the rule for the training prefixes; issue restore requests for objects the next training run needs (Standard or Bulk tier, bulk is cheaper but slower: verify current pricing and hours).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: access pattern misjudged (reads span 6 months); InvalidObjectState because archived objects must be restored before GET; retrieval fees plus restored-copy storage; early-delete or minimum-duration fees.
  4. How I'd verify: S3 access logs or Storage Lens by prefix and age; Athena over server access logs for GET counts by key age.
  5. Root cause: The decision was made from "data is old" instead of "data is read". Glacier Flexible is an archive tier, not a cheaper Standard.
  6. Fix: Short term: restore needed prefixes. Long term: Standard-IA or Glacier Instant Retrieval for 30 to 180 days (millisecond access, per-GB retrieval fee), archive only beyond the real read horizon (for example 12 months), or Intelligent-Tiering for unpredictable prefixes. Compact small files before tiering, since per-object overheads matter.
  7. Prevention: Tiering decisions require an access histogram; stage the rule on one prefix first; alerts on retrieval cost.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mass-restore everything to be "safe" (restore requests and temporary copies cost money); I would not rely on Intelligent-Tiering for tiny objects because of per-object monitoring fees (verify).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Savings math? -> Standard 200,000 GB x 0.023 = $4,600; IA at 0.0125 = $2,500; Glacier tiers lower still, but only if reads are rare.
  • Can the lifecycle change be undone cheaply? -> Transition back requires restore and copy; one-way in cost terms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an analytics team archived a year of logs and then needed them for a security investigation; restore took 12 hours and cost more than a month of savings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only removes the rule.
  • Hire: restores, picks IA or Instant Retrieval, uses access data.
  • Strong hire: staged rollout, cost breakeven, per-object fees, detection and governance.

questions.contextHtml:
Image-heavy app. Monthly AWS bill jumps from $4k to $19k. Cost Explorer: the whole increase is "Data Transfer Out" from S3 and CloudFront origin fetches. CloudFront cache hit ratio dropped from 96% to 41% three weeks ago. A release that week changed image URLs to use S3 presigned GET URLs (1 hour expiry) behind CloudFront for "privacy".

GET /u/42/cat.jpg?X-Amz-Signature=a91f...&X-Amz-Date=20261105T101500Z
GET /u/42/cat.jpg?X-Amz-Signature=77c2...&X-Amz-Date=20261105T111500Z

Egress price about $0.09/GB.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the spike and fix it without exposing private images.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase CDN TTL." The TTL is irrelevant when every URL is unique.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is CloudFront cache key including the query string? Are images really private per user or just not listable? Same image fetched by many users or one?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop generating per-request presigned URLs for public-ish assets; temporarily exclude signature params from the CDN cache key if the origin validates them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: signature in the query string makes each URL a distinct cache key; short expiry means a new URL each hour even for one user; CloudFront forwarding all query strings; cache-control missing at origin.
  4. How I'd verify: CloudFront cache statistics report, X-Cache: Miss from cloudfront headers, count distinct URLs per object in access logs. Math: extra egress $15,000 / 0.09 = about 167 TB per month, consistent with the hit ratio falling from 96% to 41% (origin traffic rose from 4% to 59% of bytes, about 15x).
  5. Root cause: Authorization was implemented in the URL, which also defines the cache key, so the cache was defeated and every view went to S3 and out to the internet.
  6. Fix: Use CloudFront signed cookies or signed URLs with a policy where the cache key excludes the signature (the CDN validates the signature at the edge and caches by path). Content-hashed keys with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for public images; keep S3 private behind Origin Access Control.
  7. Prevention: Alert on hit ratio under 90%, a cost anomaly alert, load test URLs for cache behaviour before release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the bucket public to dodge signing; for truly private content, shorter edge TTL plus signed cookies trades a lower hit ratio for revocation speed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just cache per user? -> Fragmentation: each user pays the miss once; fine for private media, wasteful for shared assets.
  • Use another vendor? -> Cloudflare R2 markets zero egress fees but you still need caching and auth design.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a feature flag for "secure images" quietly added a timestamp to image URLs, and the CDN bill tripled before anyone looked at hit ratio.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks TTL only.
  • Hire: spots unique URLs and cache key, proposes signed cookies/URLs at the CDN.
  • Strong hire: quantifies egress, separates public versus private assets, adds guardrails and alerts.

questions.promptHtml: In an S3-like system, why is the metadata service the hard part, and what does strong read-after-write consistency change for clients?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who see object stores as "disks in the cloud" from those who understand the index and consistency problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Bytes are easy to spread and replicate, but every key needs a lookup that must be correct, fast and sharded across billions or trillions of entries, including ordered LIST by prefix. That index must be strongly consistent or clients see missing or stale objects. Since December 2020 S3 gives read-after-write for PUT, DELETE and LIST, so clients no longer need retry-until-visible hacks or external consistency layers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
PUT key -> store chunks on N nodes -> commit (bucket,key,version,checksum,chunk map) in metadata
GET key -> metadata lookup -> read chunks -> verify checksum

The metadata store must shard by key range or hash, replicate with consensus, survive partition splits and support ordered range scans for LIST. Hot prefixes concentrate load on one shard; per-prefix limits (at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix) exist because of this partitioning. Commit order matters: write chunks durably first, publish metadata last, so a crash leaves orphan chunks (garbage collected) but never a key pointing at missing data. Before strong consistency, overwrite and delete were eventually consistent, so a reader could see an old version; frameworks like EMRFS consistent view or S3Guard existed to patch this. Consistency does not make a bucket a database: no transactions across keys, no conditional multi-object updates; check the provider's conditional-write support (verify).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "S3 is eventually consistent" from old material.
  • Treating LIST as cheap or as a query engine.
  • Assuming strong consistency means atomic multi-object operations.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens on crash between chunk write and metadata commit? -> Orphan chunks, cleaned by background garbage collection.
  2. Why are most outages metadata related? -> It is the shared, stateful, coordination-heavy part; data nodes are replaceable.
  3. How would you build a "rename folder"? -> Copy plus delete every key under the prefix; not atomic; design keys to avoid renames.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer describes replicas. The senior discusses write ordering (data then metadata), shard hot spots, consensus, garbage collection of orphans and what consistency does and does not guarantee.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Hadoop pipeline on pre-2020 S3 occasionally read half-listed output directories after a job; teams added manifest files, a habit that remains useful for atomic dataset publishing.

questions.contextHtml:
A mobile config service stores config/latest.json in S3 and clients fetch it directly on app start. After a push notification campaign, 40k devices open the app within a minute: about 12k GET/s for a single key. Errors:

503 Slow Down  (Code: SlowDown)  rate=38%
p99 latency 2.4 s, up from 60 ms

Same bucket also serves user uploads without issue on other prefixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Randomize key prefixes." That advice is obsolete and does not help one hot object that must keep one name.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the config the same for all clients? How stale can it be? Is a CDN in front? Does the app retry aggressively?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a CDN in front or enable client jittered backoff; temporarily raise Cache-Control: max-age=60 so repeated fetches stop hitting origin.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: single key above per-prefix request limits (about 5,500 GET/s per prefix); client retry storm making it worse; slow-down from a bucket-wide issue (unlikely since other prefixes fine); network limits at one NAT.
  4. How I'd verify: S3 request metrics by prefix (if enabled), CloudWatch 5xx, CDN hit ratio; check the retry code.
  5. Root cause: A read-mostly, identical object served direct from origin to a synchronized crowd; retries without jitter multiplied load.
  6. Fix: CloudFront (or any CDN) in front with max-age of 30 to 60 s plus stale-while-revalidate; origin sees about one request per edge per TTL. Client: exponential backoff with jitter, fetch with ETag/If-None-Match, stagger startup fetch. For campaigns, also pre-warm. Math: 12k/s at 95% hit ratio becomes 600/s at origin, far under the limit.
  7. Prevention: Load test with the notification fan-out shape; alarm on SlowDown 503 counts; version the config key (config/v123.json) with a tiny pointer to avoid purge needs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shard latest.json into 10 copies as the real fix (clients would still need a CDN-like picker); the cost is config staleness up to the TTL.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need instant config updates? -> Short TTL plus purge or versioned URL announced through push.
  • What if it were 12k PUT/s on one key? -> Per-key write rate has no good answer; buffer and batch writes, use a database or log.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 10-line client change that retried on any non-200 amplified a 5% error rate into a 4x request spike until jitter and CDN were added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random prefixes.
  • Hire: CDN, backoff, caching.
  • Strong hire: limits arithmetic, retry-storm analysis, versioned keys, test of fan-out shape.

questions.contextHtml: A photo-sharing company stores 50 PB in S3 Standard at list price about $0.023/GB-month, roughly $1.15M/month before discounts and egress. The CFO asks whether to build an own storage system (like Dropbox did) on rented or owned servers. Team: 40 engineers, none with storage-systems experience. Growth: 40%/year.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend and how do you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Own hardware is cheaper, do it." It compares raw $/GB only and ignores engineering cost, durability engineering and migration risk.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the actual negotiated S3 price and egress share? Hot/cold split? Durability and compliance needs? Is there an exit for photos older than 1 year (cold tier)? What is the opportunity cost of those engineers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not urgent; first pull cheap levers: tiering (cold photos to IA or archive tiers), dedup, re-encoding, CDN to cut egress, committed-use discount.
  3. Hypotheses (options): stay and optimize; hybrid (cold data to cheaper cloud or own storage, hot in S3); full build with EC (for example 10+4 = 1.4x).
  4. How I'd verify: Model total cost: hardware (disks, servers, networking, power, colo), 1.4x overhead from EC, spare capacity, a storage team of 8 to 12 engineers and on-call, migration egress fees. Assume own all-in cost of something like $0.004 to $0.007/GB-month (verify with quotes); 50 PB x 1.4 raw is 70 PB of disk. Saving could be $700k to $900k/month at best, offset by 10 engineers at about $300k yearly cost each = $250k/month plus risk.
  5. Root cause of the question: Cost grows linearly with data; at petabyte scale a few cents matter.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Optimize first (tiering and CDN often cut 30 to 50%), negotiate a private pricing agreement, and only consider a hybrid for cold, rarely read data using an S3-compatible system (MinIO or Ceph) to keep clients unchanged. Revisit full build beyond about 100 PB with a dedicated team.
  7. Prevention: Keep the object API abstraction so storage is swappable; keep copies in open formats; quarterly cost review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Full build is a one-way door in staffing and operations: durability incidents are existential. I would not start without an experienced storage lead and a staged migration (shadow writes, verify checksums, shift reads, then retire).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dropbox did it, why not us? -> They had exabyte-scale growth, a dedicated hardware team and a long runway; the break-even scales with data size and team.
  • What about egress fees on migration? -> Often the largest one-off cost; negotiate or use provider migration programs (verify).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a company built its own store and saved money at scale, but a firmware bug corrupted drives in one batch and the durability engineering took a year to mature.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raw $/GB comparison.
  • Hire: includes people cost and cheaper levers.
  • Strong hire: TCO model with explicit assumptions, staged hybrid path, flags the one-way door and durability risk.
